title: Fed rate hike announcement on bank stock returns

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
Event Study methodology. I will calculate abnormal returns using the market model with pre-estimated betas, then compute cumulative abnormal returns (CAR) for the [-1,+1] event window. The key assumption is that the market model adequately captures expected returns in the absence of the event, and that the rate hike announcement was unexpected by the market.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(dplyr)
library(readr)

# Read the data
data <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s11_data.csv")

# Step 1: Calculate abnormal returns using market model
# AR_it = R_it - (alpha_i + beta_i * R_mt)
# We need to estimate alpha for each stock using estimation window [-10, -2]

# Estimate alpha for each stock using estimation window
estimation_window <- data %>%
  filter(event_day >= -10 & event_day <= -2)

# Calculate alpha for each stock (intercept from market model)
alphas <- estimation_window %>%
  group_by(stock_id) %>%
  summarise(
    alpha = mean(ret - beta * mkt_ret),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Merge alphas back to main data
data <- data %>%
  left_join(alphas, by = "stock_id")

# Step 2: Calculate abnormal returns for all days
data <- data %>%
  mutate(
    expected_ret = alpha + beta * mkt_ret,
    abnormal_ret = ret - expected_ret
  )

# Step 3: Calculate CAR for event window [-1, +1]
event_window_data <- data %>%
  filter(event_day >= -1 & event_day <= 1)

# Calculate CAR for each stock
cars <- event_window_data %>%
  group_by(stock_id) %>%
  summarise(
    car_minus1_plus1 = sum(abnormal_ret),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Step 4: Test statistical significance
# Calculate mean CAR and test if significantly different from zero
mean_car <- mean(cars$car_minus1_plus1)
std_car <- sd(cars$car_minus1_plus1)
n_stocks <- nrow(cars)
se_car <- std_car / sqrt(n_stocks)
t_stat <- mean_car / se_car
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df = n_stocks - 1)

# Print main results
cat("=== EVENT STUDY RESULTS ===\n")
cat("Event Window: [-1, +1] days\n")
cat("Number of banks:", n_stocks, "\n")
cat("Mean CAR:", round(mean_car, 4), "\n")
cat("Standard Error:", round(se_car, 4), "\n")
cat("t-statistic:", round(t_stat, 3), "\n")
cat("p-value:", round(p_value, 4), "\n")
cat("95% Confidence Interval: [", round(mean_car - 1.96*se_car, 4), ", ", 
    round(mean_car + 1.96*se_car, 4), "]\n")

# Robustness check 1: Day-by-day abnormal returns
daily_ar <- event_window_data %>%
  group_by(event_day) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_ar = mean(abnormal_ret),
    t_stat = mean(abnormal_ret) / (sd(abnormal_ret) / sqrt(n())),
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

cat("\n=== DAILY ABNORMAL RETURNS ===\n")
print(daily_ar)

# Robustness check 2: Alternative event windows
alt_windows <- list(
  "[-1,0]" = c(-1, 0),
  "[0,+1]" = c(0, 1),
  "[-2,+2]" = c(-2, 2)
)

cat("\n=== ALTERNATIVE EVENT WINDOWS ===\n")
for(window_name in names(alt_windows)) {
  window_days <- alt_windows[[window_name]]
  alt_data <- data %>%
    filter(event_day >= window_days[1] & event_day <= window_days[2])
  
  alt_cars <- alt_data %>%
    group_by(stock_id) %>%
    summarise(car = sum(abnormal_ret), .groups = 'drop')
  
  alt_mean_car <- mean(alt_cars$car)
  alt_se <- sd(alt_cars$car) / sqrt(nrow(alt_cars))
  alt_t_stat <- alt_mean_car / alt_se
  
  cat("Window", window_name, "- Mean CAR:", round(alt_mean_car, 4), 
      "t-stat:", round(alt_t_stat, 3), "\n")
}

# Final summary
if(p_value < 0.05) {
  cat("\n=== CONCLUSION ===\n")
  if(mean_car > 0) {
    cat("SIGNIFICANT POSITIVE abnormal returns detected for bank stocks\n")
  } else {
    cat("SIGNIFICANT NEGATIVE abnormal returns detected for bank stocks\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("\n=== CONCLUSION ===\n")
  cat("NO SIGNIFICANT abnormal returns detected for bank stocks\n")
}
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect to find **positive** CARs with a magnitude between **2-4%** in the [-1,+1] window. Banks typically benefit from rising interest rates through improved net interest margins and higher profitability expectations. The positive effect should be most pronounced on the announcement day (day 0) with some anticipation on day -1. The magnitude reflects that rate hikes are generally favorable for traditional banking business models, though the effect size depends on how unexpected the announcement was.

_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Bank stocks show negative CAR around the rate hike announcement
